prompt.context: Our client is a mid-to-large size hospital in California. The hospital is struggling with falling profitability, and has asked us to help improve its margins.
prompt.question: The hospital has falling profitability. Revenues are falling because patients and insurers are willing to pay less, and fewer patients are coming in. The hospital has tried increasing patients by improving its branding and service offerings without much success, and all competitors are facing the same scenario due to the changing nature of the industry. Your task is to identify how the hospital can improve its margins, with a focus on the cost side.

clarifying_info.q: How is the hospital's supply chain / procurement set up?
clarifying_info.a: It is decentralized — doctors order parts like pacemakers, artificial hips, etc. directly from vendors as and when they need them.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a difference in the quality of supplies ordered from different vendors?
clarifying_info.a: No, there is no difference in the quality of the different supplies.
No, the hospital is not managed by professionals.

exhibits.title: Hip Replacements — Artificial Hip Prices by Surgeon Group
exhibits.shows: A table showing the distribution of artificial hip orders across surgeon groups, each ordering from a different vendor at a different price point, along with the total number of surgeons and procedures performed per year.

framework: Revenues: number of patients (insured vs. uninsured), average price paid by insurance/patients per procedure, number of days of hospital stay, price per night, pro bono patients

Costs: doctors & nurses, administrative staff, malpractice insurance, equipment & maintenance, ambulances, basic medical supplies (gloves, scalpels, etc.), high-tech medical supplies (pacemakers, stents, artificial hips, etc.), supply chain / sourcing
Other factors: competition in area, brand value of hospital & doctors, service quality, relationship with insurers
Since revenues are falling and external factors are industry-wide, focus analysis on cost reduction — particularly procurement / supply chain for high-cost medical supplies

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what conclusions can you draw from the hip replacement data? Note that there are about 30 basic procedures like hip replacements with similar costs and ordering patterns.
questions.guidance: A strong answer: (1) calculates total hip replacements per year; (2) computes total current spend by price tier; (3) identifies that centralizing procurement at the $1,400 price point (used by 50% of surgeons and acceptable quality) would eliminate the premium paid by the 20%+20% using $2,000/$2,200 hips; (4) quantifies the annual savings; (5) extrapolates across 30 procedures.

math.setup: Total hip replacements per year = 25 surgeons × 20 procedures each = 500. Compute total expense and potential saving per price tier, then sum savings and extrapolate.
steps: Total savings on hip replacements = $60,000 + $80,000 = $140,000 per year
Total savings across 30 similar procedures = $140,000 × 30 = $4,200,000 per year
math.answer: Centralizing procurement at $1,400 saves $140,000/year on hip replacements alone, and approximately $4.2 million/year across all 30 procedures.

brainstorming.prompt: What potential costs should the hospital consider when thinking about improving profitability?

categories.name: Supply Chain / Sourcing
ideas: Vendor fragmentation driving up unit costs

recommendation: The hospital should institute a centralized purchasing department responsible for ordering expensive implantable parts such as artificial hips, stents, heart valves, and pacemakers
This will eliminate price fragmentation across surgeons and vendors, saving an estimated $4.2 million annually across 30 procedures
Bulk ordering will also enable further price negotiation beyond the baseline savings calculated
risks: Some vendor relationships may be damaged when contracts are consolidated
Surgeons may object to losing control over their preferred vendors and, in extreme cases, may leave the hospital
A centralized purchasing team may lack the technical knowledge surgeons have about specific product specifications and clinical suitability
next_steps: Design and stand up a formal inventory management system to ensure availability of parts when needed
Engage surgeons early in the vendor selection process to gain buy-in and retain clinical input
Conduct similar analysis across other cost categories (labor, equipment, administrative) to identify additional savings levers
